# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is a good follow-up. It does what the earlier papers recommended: registered analyses, a two-year horizon, a second hours measure, and direct engagement with the critiques. Its headline conclusions are defensible. The arithmetic largely checks out. But there are some important problems:
- the summary compares two different hours measures;
- the log-hours figures are hard to reconcile with the reported cut in meetings;
- control offices that changed their own practices could explain part of the apparent decay;
- the mediation result is weaker evidence than "confirms" suggests.

## Arithmetic check

These figures reproduce:
- **Varden per-hour gains:** 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8% on timesheets, and 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5% on logs.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, a fall of 13.4%, and 96.8 / 86.6 = +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Decline in the timesheet gain:** 12.5 → 9.8 is a fall of 22%, matching "about a quarter".
- **Counter-arm staffing:** restoring coverage needs about (1 / 1.067) / 0.83 ≈ 1.13 times the staff, consistent with "12% more".
- **Counter-arm cost:** a 12% rise in staff cost becomes a 9% rise in cost per contact only if staff make up about 75% of costs. That assumption should be stated.

## 1. The summary compares two different hours measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". The 12.5% is measured on timesheets and the 8.5% on system logs. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8% (Section 3 and Section 5 both use it). Mixing the two makes the decline look like about a third instead of about a quarter.

The summary should report the timesheet figures, with 8.5% given separately as the stricter measure.

## 2. The log-hours figures don't reconcile with the meeting cut

The text defines log time as time "working on cases" in the case-management system. That would normally exclude meetings. If so, the numbers conflict:
- Timesheet hours fell 12%, about 4.5 hours a week from a baseline near 37.9.
- Meeting time fell by about 3.3 hours relative to control (treated 7.4 → 3.9, control 7.2 → 7.0).
- So meetings account for most of the timesheet reduction, and non-meeting time fell only about 1.2 hours.
- Case-work time measured by logs should then fall roughly 4%, not 11%. An 11% fall in case-work time (about 3.4 hours) plus the 3.3-hour meeting cut adds up to about 6.7 hours. That is more than the timesheet fall, which contradicts the statement that logs "show slightly more work than timesheets".

The figures fit only if log time includes time logged in during meetings. This needs clarifying, because it changes what the mediation result means (point 4). Two further questions:
- **Baseline log data:** the 24-month log estimate is a difference-in-differences, so it needs pre-period log data. Were logs available retrospectively?
- **Baseline meeting and fatigue data:** the nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. Where do the baseline meeting figures (7.4 and 7.2) and the baseline fatigue scores come from?

## 3. Control offices that cut meetings could explain part of the "decay"

From month 15, two control offices cut standing meetings, plausibly after the nine-month meetings finding circulated within the county. Their output per hour rose 4.1%. That contaminates the control arm.

Spread across seven control offices, it raises the control mean by about 1.2 points. That is close to half of the 2.7-point decline from 12.5% to 9.8%. Part of the apparent fading may therefore be the control group improving, not the treatment effect weakening. Two analyses would show this:
- a sensitivity analysis that excludes these two offices, or models the change in them directly;
- the monthly trajectory of the per-hour gain, which would show whether the decline happened gradually or around month 15. That shape also matters for whether the gain is levelling off or still falling.

There is a further inconsistency. If two of seven control offices cut meetings from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, the control average should drop about 0.6 hours. The report says it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Either the other control offices increased their meetings, or the figures refer to different periods; this should be explained.

## 4. The mediation result is weaker than "confirms" suggests

**It is not an independent replication.** The test was registered at month 11, after the nine-month association was known. It uses the same seven treated offices over a longer period. Registration prevents choosing the analysis to fit the data, but it does not provide new data.

**More office-months do not add much information.** The randomised unit is still 7 versus 7 offices. Repeated months within an office are strongly correlated. It is worth checking whether the 28–66% interval accounts for that clustering with appropriate small-sample methods.

**Neither mediator was randomised.** Offices whose managers cut meetings may differ in other ways, such as management quality. The Limitations section notes this assumption, so the wording in Sections 1, 3 and 5 should be adjusted to match: "survives a registered test" is accurate, while "confirms" is too strong.

**The meetings pathway may be partly an accounting identity.** If log hours include meeting time, cutting unproductive meetings raises output per hour by definition. That is still a substantive finding: the gain comes from removing low-value time. But it is a decomposition of the gain, not evidence of a causal mechanism. If log hours exclude meetings, the 47% result needs a different explanation, such as fewer interruptions improving focus. Either way, clarifying the log definition determines which reading applies.

## 5. Halden follow-up

**Non-response.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations agreed to take part. Organisations that reverted or struggled may have been less willing, so the reversion count (3 of 14) is probably a lower bound.

**The reversions are framed loosely.** The summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations". The marketing agency reverted over client deadlines. That is a discretionary-work failure, not a coverage one, and it slightly contradicts the clean split between the two types of work. It should be reported as such.

**Baseline hours.** The 40.3 baseline is the figure for the 27 time-tracking organisations in the re-analysis. Is it also the baseline for these 11 organisations? The 17-organisation subset had a baseline of 40.4, so the subset's own baseline should be used.

The "upper bound" framing for this group is appropriate.

## 6. Bearing on the earlier claims

**On the re-analysis.** The rebuttal is largely fair. The Varden estimate meets the standards the re-analysis recommended and still finds a gain. Two caveats apply:
- The re-analysis linked novelty to Halden's *volunteer* setting, where the change was "chosen and welcomed". Varden assigned the schedule at random, so its persistence speaks less directly to that population.
- The re-analysis predicted that *energy* would return to baseline around month ten. My calculation earlier put it closer to month nine. It did not predict that the output gain would vanish by then, so "the gain falling to zero by month ten" slightly sharpens the claim being rebutted.

**On the meta-analysis.** The report finds that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms the confound I flagged in my review of the meta-analysis, and it is an important correction.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Unchanged reporting gaps.** Resignations and appeal overturns are still reported as levels without intervals. Sick days are not normalised per scheduled day.
- **Conflicts of interest.** The authors include a Halden pilot author and the Varden trial team, who are partly evaluating critiques of their own work. A conflict-of-interest statement would help.
- **The follow-up protocol was filed at month 11.** Some design choices were made knowing the nine-month results: adding log hours and choosing output per log hour as the single outcome. These are sensible choices, but they should be acknowledged.

## Where the sequence now stands

| Question | Current answer |
|---|---|
| Size of the per-hour gain | Real but modest: about 8–10% on the best measures at two years, down from about 12.5% at nine months. Part of the decline may come from control offices adopting similar changes. |
| Decay | Partial. Neither "no decay" (the meta-analysis) nor "entirely novelty" (the re-analysis) holds. |
| Coverage-bound work | Clearly unfavourable. Varden ended its counter arm, and the Halden reverters fit the pattern, with one exception. |
| Mechanism | Removing meeting time is the leading candidate, pending clarification of what log hours measure. The two control offices raise the open question of whether that gain is available without cutting hours. |
